questions: cm1
`count(d, sex)` shows "M", "male", "Male " and "F". What should you do before you tabulate sex?
Drop the rows with the uncommon spellings
Recode them to two labels, then count again
Convert sex to a number from 1 to 4
Leave them; R groups similar labels together
Standardise the labels (case_when(), str_trim()) and re-run count(): anything not matched shows up as NA instead of being hidden.
cm2
`as.numeric("7.2 g")` returns NA. Which call reads the number 7.2?
`as.integer("7.2 g")`
`str_trim("7.2 g")`
`parse_number("7.2 g")`
`factor("7.2 g")`
parse_number() reads the first number in the text and drops the unit; look at what still becomes NA before accepting it.
cm3
Some ages are recorded as 999, a code for unknown. What is the right fix?
Set them to NA and report how many
Replace 999 with the mean age
Delete those rows from the data
Keep 999; summary() skips it
A placeholder is a missing value: set it to NA (na_if()), keep the rest of the row, and count it in the cleaning log.
cm4
Two rows share pt_id 104 but have different SBP values. What should you do first?
Keep the first row and drop the second
Check the source forms to see why
Average the two SBP values into one
Remove both rows from the analysis
Rows with the same ID and different values are not exact duplicates: they may be a repeat visit, a re-entry or a wrong ID.
it1
What does `mutate(across(c(sbp, dbp), \(x) x / 10))` do?
Creates one new column called x
Divides both columns by 10
Divides only the first column by 10
Returns the mean of the two columns
across() applies the same function to each listed column; inside mutate() it replaces those columns.
it2
`v <- "sbp"`. Which code returns the sbp column of `ncd`?
`ncd$v`
`ncd["v"]`
`ncd$"v"`
`ncd[[v]]`
ncd[[v]] uses the value stored in v; ncd$v looks for a column literally called v.
it3
Why use `map_dfr()` or `sapply()` rather than growing a vector with `res <- c(res, new)` in a loop?
They save the results to a file on disk
They return one result per item, collected
They give each test a smaller p-value
They remove missing values for you
map()/sapply() collect one result per item for you; growing a vector by hand is slow and easy to get wrong.
it4
`pct_above <- function(x, cut) mean(x >= cut, na.rm = TRUE) * 100`. What does `pct_above(c(1, 5, 10, 20), 10)` return?
Two of the four values (10 and 20) are at or above 10: 50%. Testing a function on a case with a known answer is a good habit.
bpr1
A bar chart of mean HbA1c starts its y-axis at 6.5. What is the risk?
Small differences look larger than they are
The bars become too narrow to read on screen
Colour-blind readers cannot see the bars
The legend no longer matches the colours
Bars encode values by length, so a cut axis exaggerates differences; bars should start at zero (points or lines need not).
bpr2
What does the 'gray and bold' technique do?
Prints every series in a bold black line
Greys out most data and colours the key series
Uses a grey background behind every panel
Draws every series with thick, dark lines of equal weight
Most of the data goes grey as context, and one series is highlighted, so the eye goes straight to the message.
bpr3
You compare readmission rates for 5 hospitals with long names. Which chart reads best?
A pie chart with one slice per hospital
Vertical bars with the names rotated 90°
A horizontal bar chart sorted by rate
A line chart joining the five hospitals
Horizontal bars leave room for long labels, and sorting by value makes the ranking easy to read.
bpr4
Why choose a colour-blind-safe palette such as viridis?
It makes the saved plot file much smaller
People with colour blindness can tell groups apart
It is needed by ggplot2 for more than 3 groups
It keeps colours visible on black-and-white printers
About 1 in 12 men has a colour vision deficiency; palettes like viridis stay distinguishable for them (and also in greyscale).
pd1
You want to show how HbA1c changes over 12 months in three treatment arms. Which analytical goal is this?
Ranking
Part of whole
Evolution
Flow
Change over time is the Evolution goal: lines (one per arm), with intervals if you have them.
pd2
You have one numeric variable, age. Which goal and chart fit?
Ranking: a sorted bar chart of each age
Distribution: a histogram or density plot
Part of whole: a pie chart of the ages
Correlation: a scatter plot of age against row number
One numeric variable calls for its distribution: a histogram, density, box or violin plot.
pd3
Why does the deck warn against dual-axis charts?
They can mislead through the choice of scales
They take too long to render in R
They cannot show more than 10 points
They need a colour-blind-safe palette to work well
Either axis can be stretched to suggest a link between the two series; faceting or two panels is safer.
pd4
A scatter plot of 20,000 patients is a solid blob. Which fix does the deck suggest?
A pie chart of the patients by age
Transparency, jitter, hexbin or density
A 3D scatter plot rotated to a better angle
A dual-axis chart with two y-scales
Overplotting hides density; alpha, jitter, hexbins or 2D density show where the points are concentrated.
ga1
In `ggplot(ncd, aes(x = age, y = sbp)) + geom_point()`, what does `aes()` do?
Sets a fixed colour for every point drawn
Maps columns of the data to visual properties
Chooses the type of shape to draw, here points
Loads the data from the file into R first
aes() maps variables to aesthetics (x, y, colour, size); the geom decides how they are drawn.
ga2
Which geom draws bars whose heights are values already in your data?
`geom_bar()`
`geom_histogram()`
`geom_point()`
`geom_col()`
geom_col() uses the y values as given; geom_bar() counts rows for you, and geom_histogram() bins a continuous x.
ga3
When does `geom_line()` suit the data best?
When x has unordered categories like region
When x is ordered, such as visit dates
When you want to count the rows per group
When each patient has one single value
A line implies a progression from one x to the next, which makes sense for ordered x such as time.
ga4
ExerciseFreq has 44 missing values. Which code keeps them as their own group in a bar chart?
`filter(!is.na(ExerciseFreq))`
`replace_na(ExerciseFreq, "Unknown")`
`mean(ExerciseFreq, na.rm = TRUE)`
`summarise(n = sum(is.na(ExerciseFreq)))`
replace_na() turns NA into an explicit 'Unknown' category, so the missing values stay visible instead of being dropped.
gb1
`aes(color = "blue")` gives red points and a legend that says 'blue'. Why?
ggplot2 cannot draw blue points by default
"blue" was mapped as a data value, not set
The theme overrides colours set in aes()
Colours must be given as hex codes in R
Inside aes() a constant is treated as data (one group called 'blue'); set a fixed colour outside aes(): geom_point(color = "blue").
gb2
In `facet_wrap(~ region, scales = "free_y")`, what does `free_y` do?
Removes the y-axis from every panel
Lets each panel pick its own colour scale
Lets each panel use its own y-axis range
Sorts the panels by their mean y value
Each panel gets its own y range: details show better, but panels can no longer be compared by height at a glance.
gb3
How does `facet_grid(sex ~ region)` differ from `facet_wrap(~ region)`?
facet_grid() puts one variable in rows, one in columns
facet_wrap() needs a numeric variable to split the data on
facet_grid() draws all of the groups in one panel
facet_wrap() adds a separate legend to each panel
facet_grid() crosses two variables as a grid of rows and columns; facet_wrap() wraps the panels of one variable.
gb4
Which theme removes axes, grid lines and background, as for a map?
`theme_minimal()`
`theme_classic()`
`theme_bw()`
`theme_void()`
theme_void() draws only the data layers; theme_minimal() still keeps grid lines and axis text.
pm1
Twenty hospitals each have one readmission rate. Which plot ranks them clearly with little ink?
A chord diagram of the twenty hospitals
A Cleveland dot plot or lollipop chart
A 2D density plot of the twenty rates
A radial bar chart with stacked layers
One value per category, ranked: a sorted dot or lollipop plot uses position, which we read most accurately.
pm2
Thousands of age–SBP pairs overlap into a solid block. Which plot shows where points are dense?
A pie chart of age groups
A lollipop chart of each pair
A hexbin or 2D density plot
A chord diagram of the pairs
Hexbins and 2D densities count points per area, so dense regions stand out instead of hiding under each other.
pm3
Patients move from referral stage to treatment outcome. Which plot shows those flows?
A Sankey or alluvial plot
A ridgeline plot of stages
A choropleth of the stages
A hexbin plot of each stage
Sankey and alluvial plots draw flows between stages with widths proportional to the number of patients.
mv1
You add a density curve to a histogram of counts and the curve lies flat near zero. What fixes it?
Add `alpha = 0.5` to the histogram layer
Use `y = after_stat(density)` in the histogram
Use `geom_col()` in place of `geom_histogram()`
Set `bins = 100` so the bars are narrower
A density integrates to 1 and is tiny next to counts; drawing the histogram on the density scale puts both on the same axis.
mv2
When does putting the raw points over a box plot help most?
Very large groups of 10,000 or more
When the outcome is a category
Small groups, so readers see the n
When each group has one value
With small groups a box hides how few points it summarises; the points show the n (use jitter and transparency).
mv3
You add a zoom panel to a map. What should the main map show?
A second legend for the same colours
Where the zoomed area comes from
The zoom panel's title in large type
A north arrow inside every region
Mark the zoomed area on the main map (a rectangle), so the reader knows what the detail panel shows.
ps1
A cell's standardised chi-square residual is +2.6. What does it suggest?
Fewer counts than independence predicts
The chi-square test is not valid here
More counts than independence predicts
The cell has 2.6 times the expected n
A positive residual beyond about +2 means noticeably more observations than expected under independence; it is a z-like score, not a ratio.
ps2
On a coefficient plot, a 95% CI crosses 0. What does that mean?
The effect is exactly zero in the population
The data are consistent with no effect
The model failed to converge for that term
The variable should be removed from the data
Zero is among the plausible values, so the data cannot rule out no effect; the width of the interval says how precise the estimate is.
ps3
The notches of two box plots do not overlap. What does that roughly indicate?
The means of the two groups are identical
Both groups follow a normal distribution
The groups have the same sample size
The medians likely differ (a rough 95% check)
Notches show an approximate 95% interval for each median; non-overlapping notches suggest the medians differ.
gt1
In a randomised trial, why should Table 1 not show p-values for baseline differences?
They make the table too wide to print
Any difference between arms arose by chance
gtsummary cannot compute them for trials
The groups are too small for any test
Randomisation makes the null hypothesis true by design, so a baseline p-value tests nothing useful; look at the size of differences instead.
gt2
SBP is right-skewed. Which `statistic =` setting suits it in `tbl_summary()`?
`"{mean} ({sd}) [{min}, {max}]"`
For a skewed variable the median and interquartile range describe the middle better than the mean and SD.
gt3
What does `add_p()` add to a gtsummary table?
A column of p-values, with each test footnoted
A total column that pools all of the groups
Confidence intervals for each of the group means
A row with the number of missing values per group
add_p() picks a test per variable (t-test, Wilcoxon, chi-square, Fisher) and names it in a footnote.
gt4
`tbl_regression(model_log, exponentiate = TRUE)` shows what for a logistic model?
Log-odds with standard errors
Odds ratios with 95% CIs
Predicted probabilities per row
Risk ratios with p-values
exponentiate = TRUE turns log-odds coefficients into odds ratios, with their confidence intervals.
gm1
The same 50 patients have SBP measured at baseline, 3 and 6 months. Which function fits?
`ggbetweenstats()`
`ggwithinstats()`
`ggpiestats()`
`gghistostats()`
Repeated measures on the same people need a within-subjects (paired) comparison: ggwithinstats() with subject.id.
gm2
ggstatsplot prints log(BF01) = 3.0 under a plot. What does that mean?
Strong evidence that the group means differ a lot
Strong evidence for no difference between groups
The p-value is 3.0 on a log scale
The test failed and returned no estimate
BF01 = exp(3.0) ≈ 20: the data are about 20 times more likely under 'no difference' than under 'a difference'.
gm3
When is a pie chart from `ggpiestats()` a reasonable choice?
Many categories that need exact comparison
Comparing a continuous outcome across groups
Few categories and a non-technical audience
Showing change in one group over time
Pies work for a handful of categories and a general audience; for more categories or close comparisons use ggbarstats().
da1
Foot pain was recorded before and after an intervention in the same people. Which test compares the two proportions?
Chi-square test for association
McNemar test
Chi-square goodness-of-fit
Two-sample t-test
Paired yes/no answers need McNemar's test, which uses the people who changed; a chi-square test assumes independent groups.
da2
`chisq.test(x = observed, p = c(0.5, 0.5))` on screened yes/no tests what?
Whether screening is associated with sex
Whether screening differs from a 50:50 split
Whether screening changed between two visits
Whether the screening counts are normal
With p = given, chisq.test() is a goodness-of-fit test against those proportions.
da3
Points on a Q-Q plot bend away from the line at both ends. What does that suggest?
The sample mean has been computed wrongly
The two variables are strongly correlated
The tails differ from a normal distribution
The data have no missing values in them
The ends of a Q-Q plot show the tails: curving away means heavier or lighter tails than a normal distribution.
qm1
A report declares `params: region: "North"` in its YAML. How does R code in the document read the value?
`region`
`Sys.getenv("region")`
`params$region`
`yaml$region`
Parameters are available in the document's code as the list params.
qm2
What does `quarto render report.qmd -P region:South` do?
Adds a new parameter called South to the YAML
Renders the report with region set to South
Renders only the South section of the file
Prints the value of region to the console
-P overrides a parameter for one render, so the same source gives one report per region.
qm3
Which chunk option lets you cite a table as `@tbl-baseline`?
`#| label: baseline`
`#| tbl-cap: baseline`
`#| label: tbl-baseline`
`#| fig-cap: tbl-baseline`
A label starting with tbl- (or fig-) makes the output a numbered, citable cross-reference.
qm4
To render a PDF, what does Quarto need besides R?
A Microsoft Word licence on the machine
A LaTeX installation such as TinyTeX
The pdftools package loaded in R
An internet connection during render
PDF output goes through LaTeX; tinytex::install_tinytex() installs a small distribution.
ex1
A figure for a printed journal page must stay sharp when enlarged. Which format suits it?
PNG at 72 dpi
PDF or SVG (vector)
JPEG at low quality
A screenshot of the plot
Vector formats store shapes, not pixels, so they stay sharp at any size.
ex2
After `png("fig.png")` and `plot(x)`, the file is empty. What is missing?
`ggsave()` to write the file
`print()` around the png() call
`dev.off()` to close the device
`library(grDevices)` first
Base graphics devices write the file when the device is closed with dev.off().
ex3
What resolution does the page recommend for print?
72 dpi
96 dpi
150 dpi
300 dpi
300 dpi (or more) for print; 72–150 dpi is enough on screen.
pt1
You need an interactive version of an existing ggplot `p` for a web page. Which call does that?
`lattice::xyplot(p)`
`graphics::plot(p)`
`ggplot2::ggsave(p)`
`plotly::ggplotly(p)`
ggplotly() converts a ggplot into an interactive plotly chart with tooltips and zoom.
pt2
What is `par(mfrow = c(2, 2))` for in base R?
Four colours for the points of one plot
A 2 × 2 grid of plots in one window
A plot with two y-axes on one x
Saving one plot into four files
mfrow sets a grid of rows × columns for the next base plots; reset it with par(mfrow = c(1, 1)).
pt3
In `xyplot(mpg ~ wt | factor(cyl), data = mtcars)`, what does `| factor(cyl)` do?
Draws one panel per number of cylinders
Colours the points by number of cylinders
Removes the cars with missing cylinders
Sorts the points by number of cylinders
In lattice, | conditions the plot: one panel per level, like facet_wrap() in ggplot2.
